## Sample from the CLAUDE.md

**The "What We Don't Do" section** (this is where most CLAUDE.md templates fail â€” they tell Claude what to do but not what to avoid):

| We don't do this | We do this instead | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `pages/` directory | `app/` directory | We're on Next.js 15 App Router â€” no mixing |
| UUID primary keys | CUID2 | Shorter, URL-safe, time-sortable |
| `OFFSET` pagination | Cursor-based (keyset) | OFFSET degrades at scale |
| Hard delete | Soft delete (`deletedAt`) | User data is precious; hard deletes are irreversible |
| `any` type | Drizzle inferred types + Zod | Type safety is the entire point |
| Business logic in components | `server/actions/` and `server/queries/` | Components render; servers compute |

**The schema pattern section** (gives Claude the exact template to follow every time it creates a table):

```ts
export const users = sqliteTable("users", {
  id:        text("id").primaryKey(),           // CUID2, generated at app level
  email:     text("email").notNull().unique(),
  createdAt: integer("created_at", { mode: "timestamp" }).notNull().default(sql`(unixepoch())`),
  updatedAt: integer("updated_at", { mode: "timestamp" }).notNull().default(sql`(unixepoch())`),
});
```

```ts
"use server"

  const parsed = updateUserSchema.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData));
  if (!parsed.success) return { error: parsed.error.flatten() };
  await db.update(users).set(parsed.data).where(eq(users.id, parsed.data.id));
  revalidatePath("/dashboard");
}
```

- "Use CUID2, not UUID, not auto-increment integers"
- "Paginate with `limit` + `cursor` (keyset), not OFFSET"
- "Never write raw SQL in route handlers â€” always go through `server/queries/`"
- "Return `{ error }` or `{ data }` from Server Actions â€” never throw"

Claude doesn't need to ask what "best practices" means when it has the exact pattern in front of it.

# CLAUDE.md - Next.js 15 + SQLite SaaS

> Production-ready context guide for Claude Code working on a Next.js 15 App Router + SQLite SaaS project.

## Stack & Versions

```
Next.js: 15.x (App Router)
SQLite: better-sqlite3 or @local-first/sync (Turso compatible)
Runtime: Node.js 20+
Package Manager: npm (no pnpm/yarn)
Styling: Tailwind CSS
Auth: NextAuth.js v5 with credentials or OAuth
Deployment: Vercel or Railway
```

## Project Structure

```
/
|-- app/                      # Next.js App Router pages
|   |-- (auth)/             # Auth routes (login, register, forgot)
|   |-- (dashboard)/        # Protected dashboard routes
|   |-- api/                # API Route Handlers
|   |   |-- auth/           # NextAuth endpoints
|   |   |-- [resource]/     # RESTful resource handlers
|   |-- layout.tsx
|-- components/
|   |-- ui/                 # Shadcn/ui primitives only
|   |-- forms/              # React Hook Form + Zod schemas
|   |-- features/            # Feature-specific components
|-- lib/
|   |-- db/                 # Database client + migrations
|   |   |-- client.ts       # better-sqlite3 instance
|   |   |-- migrations/     # SQL migration files
|   |-- auth/               # Auth utilities
|   |-- utils.ts            # Shared helpers
|-- scripts/                 # DB seed / migrate scripts
|-- CLAUDE.md               # <- You are here
```

**Key rule**: Never put business logic in app/api/*.ts directly. Always go through lib/ modules.

## Naming Conventions

| Thing | Convention | Example |
|-------|------------|---------|
| Pages | kebab-case | app/users/page.tsx |
| Components | PascalCase | UserCard.tsx |
| Server actions | camelCase | createUser() |
| Database tables | snake_case | user_accounts |
| API routes | kebab-case | app/api/user-profile/route.ts |
| CSS classes | Tailwind only | className="text-lg font-medium" |

## SQL / Migration Conventions

### Migrations

1. All schema changes via migration files in lib/db/migrations/
2. 2. Naming: 0001_add_users.sql, 0002_add_sessions.sql, etc.
3. 3. **Never run DROP or ALTER in production migrations** - only additive changes
4. 4. Use better-sqlite3's synchronous API for server components; async for API routes
### Query Patterns

```typescript
// V DO: Use parameterized queries, never string interpolation
const user = db.prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?').get(userId)

// X DON'T: String interpolation allows SQL injection
const user = db.prepare(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${userId}`).get()
```

### Transactions

```typescript
// Wrap multi-step operations in transactions
const result = db.transaction(() => {
  const user = db.prepare('INSERT INTO users ...').run(...);
  db.prepare('INSERT INTO sessions ...').run(...);
  return user;
})();
```

## Component Patterns

### Server vs Client Components

- app/ files with use client = interactive UI only
- - Everything else = Server Component by default
- - - **Never** fetch data in client components - use Server Components + fetch() with cache
### Form Handling

```typescript
// V DO: React Hook Form + Zod everywhere
const schema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  password: z.string().min(8),
});
const form = useForm<z.infer<typeof schema>>({ resolver: zodResolver(schema) });

// X DON'T: useState for form state
// X DON'T: uncontrolled inputs for anything beyond trivial forms
```

### Feature Components

Each feature gets its own folder under components/features/:

```
components/features/users/
|-- UserList.tsx         # Server Component (fetches data)
|-- UserListClient.tsx   # Client wrapper for interactivity
|-- UserCard.tsx
|-- index.ts            # Re-exports
|-- UserForm.tsx        # If needed
```

## What We Don't Do (and Why)

| Pattern | Why We Avoid It |
|---------|----------------|
| Class components | React Server Components + functional only |
| useEffect for data fetching | Server Components + actions instead |
| Inline styles | Tailwind only, consistent design system |
| npm run dev in production | Use proper deployment (Vercel/Railway) |
| Storing secrets in code | Environment variables via .env.local |
| console.log in production | Use structured logging to stdout |
| Direct db.exec() in API routes | Use typed db.prepare() with parameterization |

## Dev Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # Start development server (http://localhost:3000)
npm run db:migrate   # Run pending migrations
npm run db:seed      # Seed development database
npm run build        # Production build
npm run lint         # ESLint check
npm run type-check   # tsc --noEmit
```

## API Response Pattern

All API routes return this shape:

```typescript
// app/api/example/route.ts
export async function GET(request: Request) {
  try {
    const data = await getExampleData();
    return Response.json({ ok: true, data });
  } catch (error) {
    return Response.json(
      { ok: false, error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Unknown error' },
      { status: 400 }
    );
  }
}
```

- - - X Storing plain-text passwords (must be hashed with bcrypt/argon2)
- - - - X Returning raw database rows as API responses (always validate + transform)
- - - - - X any type annotations (use unknown + type guards instead)

# CLAUDE.md — Next.js 15 + SQLite SaaS

## Stack & Versions

- **Next.js 15** (App Router, Server Components by default)
- **React 19** (RC or stable)
- **TypeScript 5** (strict mode enabled)
- **Tailwind CSS 4** (utility-first, no arbitrary values in production)
- **better-sqlite3** (local SQLite) OR **@libsql/client** (Turso/cloud)
- **Drizzle ORM** (preferred over raw SQL for type safety)
- **Zod** (runtime validation, always validate at API boundary)
- **NextAuth.js v5** (Auth.js) or **Lucia** (if rolling custom auth)

> **Why this stack:** SQLite is sufficient for 95% of SaaS apps until 100k+ users. 
> Drizzle gives type-safe SQL without the Prisma black box. Next.js 15 App Router 
> eliminates API boilerplate via Server Actions.

---

## Folder Structure

```
my-saas/
├── app/                    # Next.js App Router
│   ├── (auth)/             # Route groups (no URL segment)
│   │   ├── login/
│   │   └── register/
│   ├── (dashboard)/        # Authenticated routes
│   │   ├── layout.tsx      # Auth guard + sidebar
│   │   ├── page.tsx        # Dashboard home
│   │   └── settings/
│   ├── api/                # Route handlers (rarely needed)
│   ├── layout.tsx          # Root layout (providers, fonts)
│   └── globals.css
├── components/
│   ├── ui/                 # shadcn/ui components (never edit directly)
│   ├── forms/              # Form-specific components
│   └── features/           # Domain-specific (e.g., BillingTable)
├── lib/
│   ├── db/                 # Database layer
│   │   ├── schema.ts       # Drizzle schema (single source of truth)
│   │   ├── migrations/     # Generated by drizzle-kit
│   │   └── index.ts        # DB client singleton
│   ├── auth.ts             # Auth configuration
│   └── utils.ts            # cn() helper, general utilities
├── hooks/                  # Custom React hooks
├── types/                  # Global TypeScript types (rarely needed)
└── public/                 # Static assets
```

> **Why:** Route groups keep URLs clean while co-locating related pages. 
> The `lib/db/` directory is the ONLY place SQL lives. No queries in components.

---

## SQL / Migration Conventions

### Schema Rules
1. **Single file:** All tables in `lib/db/schema.ts`
2. **Naming:** `snake_case` for DB columns, `camelCase` in TypeScript (Drizzle maps them)
3. **Timestamps:** Every table gets `created_at` and `updated_at` (use `defaultNow()`)
4. **Soft deletes:** Use `deleted_at` (nullable timestamp) instead of `DELETE` for user data
5. **Foreign keys:** Always define with `onDelete: 'cascade'` or `'set null'` explicitly
6. **Indexes:** Add indexes on every foreign key and frequently queried column

### Migration Workflow
```bash
# 1. Modify schema.ts
# 2. Generate migration
npx drizzle-kit generate

# 3. Review the generated SQL in migrations/ folder
# 4. Apply to local DB
npx drizzle-kit migrate

# 5. For Turso production
npx drizzle-kit push:sqlite   # or turso specific command
```

> **Why:** Reviewing generated SQL catches Drizzle bugs. Never hand-write migrations 
> unless fixing a broken one. Soft deletes prevent accidental data loss and simplify GDPR.

---

## Component Patterns

### Server Components (Default)
```tsx
// app/(dashboard)/page.tsx
import { db } from '@/lib/db'
import { users } from '@/lib/db/schema'

export default async function DashboardPage() {
  // ✅ Query directly in Server Component
  const allUsers = await db.select().from(users)
  
  return <UserTable data={allUsers} />
}
```

### Client Components (Only when needed)
```tsx
'use client'

// Use ONLY for:
// - Interactivity (onClick, useState, useEffect)
// - Browser APIs (localStorage, clipboard)
// - Real-time features (WebSockets)

import { useState } from 'react'

export function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}</button>
}
```

### Server Actions
```tsx
// app/(dashboard)/actions.ts
'use server'

import { db } from '@/lib/db'
import { users } from '@/lib/db/schema'
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'
import { z } from 'zod'

const createUserSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  name: z.string().min(1),
})

export async function createUser(formData: FormData) {
  // ✅ Validate at the boundary
  const data = createUserSchema.parse({
    email: formData.get('email'),
    name: formData.get('name'),
  })
  
  await db.insert(users).values(data)
  
  // ✅ Revalidate to refresh Server Component data
  revalidatePath('/dashboard')
}
```

> **Why:** Server Components reduce client JS by 70%+. Server Actions replace 
> API routes for mutations, eliminating serialization boilerplate. Always validate 
> with Zod — never trust client input.

## What We Don't Do (And Why)

| Don't | Why |
|-------|-----|
| ❌ Use `useEffect` to fetch data on mount | Use Server Components or Server Actions instead. Eliminates loading states, race conditions, and hydration mismatches. |
| ❌ Put SQL queries in `.tsx` files outside `lib/db/` | Database logic must be centralized. Components should call functions, not write SQL. |
| ❌ Use `any` type | Disables TypeScript's value. Use `unknown` + narrowing if types are unclear. |
| ❌ Store secrets in `.env.local` only | Use `.env.local` for local dev, but verify production secrets are in Vercel/Turso dashboard. |
| ❌ Use `SELECT *` | Always select specific columns. Prevents breaking changes when adding columns. |
| ❌ Skip migrations and use `push` in production | `drizzle-kit push` can drop data. Migrations are versioned and reviewable. |
| ❌ Use `use client` at the top of every file | Default to Server Components. Only 10-20% of components need to be client-side. |
| ❌ Handle auth in every page manually | Use route group layouts `(dashboard)/layout.tsx` with auth guards. |
| ❌ Use raw SQL without Drizzle | Only acceptable in migrations or complex queries. Drizzle provides type safety and prevents SQL injection. |
| ❌ Commit `.env` files | Add `.env*.local` to `.gitignore`. Leaked secrets are irreversible. |

#### 📦 Deliverable

#### ⚙️ Features

- **Conventional Commits**: Automatically categorizes commits (Features, Bug Fixes, Docs, etc.).
- **Single File**: No external dependencies, just `python generate_changelog.py`.
- **Customizable**: Configurable commit limit and output path.

#### 🛠️ Usage

## [2026-03-31]

#### 📄 Full Script Code
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Generate a structured CHANGELOG.md from Git history.
Usage: python generate_changelog.py [--format markdown|json|text] [--output CHANGELOG.md]
"""

import subprocess
import json
import re
import argparse
from datetime import datetime
from typing import List, Dict

def get_git_log(limit: int = 100) -> List[Dict]:
    """Fetch git log with structured data"""
    cmd = [
        "git", "log", f"-{limit}", "--pretty=format:%H|%an|%ae|%ad|%s",
        "--date=short"
    ]
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    
    entries = []
    for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
        if not line:
            continue
        parts = line.split("|")
        if len(parts) >= 5:
            entries.append({
                "hash": parts[0],
                "author": parts[1],
                "email": parts[2],
                "date": parts[3],
                "message": parts[4]
            })
    return entries

def categorize_commit(message: str) -> str:
    """Categorize commit based on conventional commits"""
    msg = message.lower()
    if any(kw in msg for kw in ["feat", "add", "new", "implement"]):
        return "Features"
    elif any(kw in msg for kw in ["fix", "bug", "patch", "resolve"]):
        return "Bug Fixes"
    elif any(kw in msg for kw in ["docs", "doc", "readme", "comment"]):
        return "Documentation"
    elif any(kw in msg for kw in ["refactor", "restructure", "clean"]):
        return "Refactoring"
    elif any(kw in msg for kw in ["test", "spec"]):
        return "Tests"
    elif any(kw in msg for kw in ["chore", "build", "ci", "deploy"]):
        return "Chores"
    else:
        return "Other"

def generate_markdown(entries: List[Dict]) -> str:
    """Generate Markdown CHANGELOG"""
    lines = ["# Changelog", ""]
    
    # Group by date
    current_date = None
    for entry in entries:
        if entry["date"] != current_date:
            current_date = entry["date"]
            lines.append(f"## [{current_date}]")
            lines.append("")
        
        category = categorize_commit(entry["message"])
        short_hash = entry["hash"][:7]
        lines.append(f"- **{category}**: {entry['message']} ([`{short_hash}`](https://github.com/owner/repo/commit/{entry['hash']})) - @{entry['author']}")
    
    lines.append("")
    return "\n".join(lines)

def generate_json(entries: List[Dict]) -> str:
    """Generate JSON CHANGELOG"""
    return json.dumps({
        "version": "1.0.0",
        "generated_at": datetime.now().isoformat(),
        "entries": entries
    }, indent=2)

def generate_text(entries: List[Dict]) -> str:
    """Generate plain text CHANGELOG"""
    lines = ["CHANGELOG", "=" * 50, ""]
    for entry in entries:
        lines.append(f"[{entry['date']}] {entry['message']} - @{entry['author']}")
    lines.append("")
    return "\n".join(lines)

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Generate CHANGELOG from Git history")
    parser.add_argument("--format", choices=["markdown", "json", "text"], default="markdown", help="Output format")
    parser.add_argument("--output", default="CHANGELOG.md", help="Output file path")
    parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=100, help="Number of commits to process")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    print(f"[INFO] Fetching last {args.limit} commits...")
    entries = get_git_log(args.limit)
    
    if not entries:
        print("[ERROR] No commits found.")
        return
    
    print(f"[INFO] Generating {args.format.upper()} changelog...")
    
    if args.format == "markdown":
        content = generate_markdown(entries)
    elif args.format == "json":
        content = generate_json(entries)
    else:
        content = generate_text(entries)
    
    with open(args.output, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(content)
    
    print(f"[SUCCESS] Changelog saved to {args.output}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

## Agent Code (core logic)

```python
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a senior software engineer conducting a thorough code review.
Return ONLY valid JSON with exactly these keys:
{
  "summary": "<2-3 sentence summary>",
  "risks": ["<risk 1>", ...],
  "suggestions": ["<suggestion 1>", ...],
  "confidence": "<Low|Medium|High>"
}"""

message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-20250514",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_message}],
)
```

The agent parses Claude's JSON response and renders it as structured Markdown. Large diffs (>60,000 chars) are symmetrically truncated with a notice so context limits are never exceeded.

This is a great bounty idea. One thing we learned building a similar tool: a generic PR review agent that just summarizes changes and lists "risks" tends to produce reviews that look helpful but are actually surface-level — the kind of thing a senior dev skims and dismisses.

The reviews that actually catch real bugs are the ones that check for failure modes specific to AI-generated code, which traditional review tools miss entirely:

- **Hallucinated imports** — packages that don't exist on npm/PyPI but pass type checking and unit tests because the import path is never exercised
- **Deprecated API usage** masked by version pinning in dev/staging
- **Cross-file context inconsistencies** when AI generates changes across multiple sessions (the kind of thing this issue describes — context amnesia)
- **Over-engineering** — AI adding Strategy/Factory patterns to features that need none, passing SonarQube but killing maintainability

If anyone's building this agent, I'd suggest focusing on these AI-native blind spots rather than generic "code quality" heuristics. The latter is already well-covered by existing tools.

## Submission

**Repo:** https://github.com/daviediao-code/claude-review-agent/tree/master

**How to use:**

# Set your API key
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key-here

# Review a PR
python3 claude_review.py --pr https://github.com/sigma67/ytmusicapi/pull/938

# Save to file
python3 claude_review.py --pr https://github.com/sigma67/ytmusicapi/pull/938 --output review.md
```

**Sample review output on ytmusicapi#938:**
```
## Summary
This PR adds an optional `image: Path | None` parameter to `edit_playlist()` for setting custom playlist thumbnail images...

## Identified Risks
- Auth check is confusingly written: `if not self.auth_type == AuthType.BROWSER` uses double negation
- No file size validation: Large files will consume bandwidth before failing
- Code duplication: Resumable upload logic closely duplicates code in `uploads.py`

## Improvement Suggestions
- Extract shared `_resumable_upload()` helper into `_utils.py`
- Add client-side file size validation (10MB limit)
- Fix auth_type check to be more explicit

## Confidence Score: High
```

The agent correctly identifies code quality issues, security concerns, and provides actionable improvement suggestions.

body:
The number of tensix instructions to do a particular task can be easily optimized with human thinking, as the main task would have an algorithm and the proper instructions and sequence can often be easily chosen. But to pass on the tensix insturctions to the tensix engine, we often use MOPs and Replay buffers to pass them so that the number of RISCV instructions are rerduced. That part has too many ways of accomplishing and is not too easy to find out what is the most optimal way all the time. 

This is where we can use AI to reduce the number of RISV instructions used, by varying the possibilities of writing the MOP and arrangement of the replay buffer. Overall the task is 

Objective : Minimize the number of RISCV instructions to issue instructions to tensix engine 
Constraints : Sequence of tensix instructions passed remains the same
                       Only specified amount of replay buffer is used (for example if Math thread uses whole of the buffer, it may clash with SFPU algorithms when they are run from a separate thread on WH/BH for the buffer being shared. 
                        Take into account two ways of writing mops and their constraints. 

An AI agent may be asked to do it for all the ops we have and then we filter out the good suggestions and apply them.

comments.body: FYI @pmilenkovicTT @fvranicTT
@vvukomanovicTT  (since you are into AI kernel generation)

Hi @amahmudTT @pmilenkovicTT @fvranicTT @vvukomanovicTT,

Heads up, going to take a swing at this. I've been doing similar work on BarraCUDA (github.com/Zaneham/BarraCUDA), my open-source hobby compiler. The Tenstorrent backend emits RV32IM for the baby cores already and I've been building out the scheduler / optimiser layer, so MOP and replay-buffer minimisation sits in the same problem space.

I'll add a classical optimiser pass that searches MOP layouts and replay arrangements with thread-sharing constraints encoded, verifies functional equivalence of the Tensix stream, and minimises RISCV instruction count. Will prototype on a small set of ops first.

PR coming when I've got something to show. Will post here when it's up.

@Zaneham thanks for volunteering. The llk repo has been merged with tt-metal repo. Any PR has to be against the tt-metal repo.

Absolutely!

Thanks @Zaneham for the interest, and let us know when you have any questions or we can help with anything!

Thanks @Zaneham for the interest, the bounty is now yours! Please update this issue with your progress within 2 weeks. You will have 2 months maximum to complete this bounty, after which it will be reopened.

Review our [Bounty Terms & Conditions](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/bounty_terms.html), as these terms apply. Good luck with the project, and let us know if there are any bugs/issues on our side that are stopping you from completing the bounty. 

If you need access to Tenstorrent hardware, we can provide that for you through the cloud. Please comment asking for access once you've been assigned to the bounty if you need access.

Let me know if you have any other questions or if we can help!

Just a wee progress update.

Got the replay-buffer half of the optimiser going. I built it verifier-first, so every arrangement it suggests gets checked against the exact Tensix stream before it's allowed to count. Keeps me honest on the "same instructions out" constraint rather than just trusting myself.

So far it'll:
- spot repeated instruction blocks, load each into the replay buffer once (executing the first pass as it loads), then replay it everywhere it shows up again. Copes with a few different blocks at once, not just one.
- stay inside a buffer budget, so it won't hand you a plan that stomps on slots another thread needs. That's the Math/SFPU sharing thing from the issue. Tell it 16 slots and it behaves.
- spit out an actual do-this suggestion by offset: "record these N instructions into slots [a,b), replay there instead of those."

Gave it a real kernel to chew on: pulled the MVMUL inner block out of `llk_math_matmul.h` (non-transposed path), 15 instructions, and it folds the repeated 7-instruction run into a load plus a replay. 15 down to 10 RISC-V issues, call it a third off, and verified to come back as the identical Tensix stream. In sim mind you, not on a chip yet. I checked the execute-while-loading behaviour against `load_replay_buf` so that first-pass-as-the-load bit isn't a guess.

It's sitting on top of my open Tensix assembler (github.com/Zaneham/ttas), second piece of a toolchain I'm building out.

Where I've hit a wall, and it's the MOP half: I can't work out from the headers whether the double-loop MOP expander (`ckernel_template`) actually issues the NOP template slots, the `start_op`, the `end_op`s, an unused second loop op, or whether it just skips the NOPs. That one detail decides whether a MOP can reproduce a clean repeated stream at all, so it's holding up the whole MOP-fitting pass. If someone knows off the top of their head, that'd unblock me on the spot, no hardware needed for that one.

Separately on hardware: the Koyeb access is a known issue at the moment. I've had a go at getting it working and emailed their support, but no joy yet. So if there's another route onto a chip in the meantime I'd jump on it, just to run the optimiser's output end to end and confirm it holds up.

Cheers

@mcraigheadTT If you know the answer to the above question could you drop a line here ? From the ISA doc it seems the nops are not executed.

Hi, I can take a look, as the exact NOP behavior for MOP (which NOPs does it emit vs. which NOPs does it swallow) has been on my list of "need to understand better" for a while now. In addition to the doc there - @Zaneham , you may find it helpful to look at the MOP code in https://github.com/tenstorrent/ttsim/blob/main/src/tensix.cpp. It's essentially the same as the ISA doc, but the ISA doc being written in what I would call "pseudo-Python" for MOP (async, yield) is a bit hairy.
I'm digging into this now; some minor ISA spec updates forthcoming, but I doubt they will substantively change the conclusions in your specific cases w.r.t. when a NOP is emitted vs. when it isn't.
Finished ISA spec review and made minor edits based on my findings: https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-isa-documentation/commit/9ba1ce0ad519b2c83e5465528ae6cc237ba53560

Oh beauty, update time, and a massive thanks first.

@amahmudTT  @mcraigheadTT you legends. The NOP thing was the one wall holding up the entire MOP half and you just
sorted it. @mcraigheadTT going and actually reviewing the ISA spec over a question from some random on the internet,
that's properly above and beyond. The double-loop expander matches the documented behaviour now: NOP slots skipped,
one op per inner step, the alternation doubling the count, last step replacing instead of appending. My first crack at
it was quietly wrong in a way my own tests waltzed straight past, so the timing was perfect.

And the ttsim tip, mean. Yanked the mop/replay expander out of tensix.cpp and turned it into an oracle, so now I fuzz
my own expander against it a few thousand plans a run. If they ever disagree, ttsim wins every time, cause it's yours
and I'm just some bloke. Way better net than my hand-written tests, and it means I can trust the thing without a chip
in the loop, so the Koyeb gremlins haven't actually held me up.

Matmul's the fun bit. I can model the real config the way you actually program it now, record the block then a MOP
whose body replays it, expanded properly. Chuck the raw stream at the optimiser with zero hints and it lands on the
exact same record-once-replay trick the kernel hand-codes. 64 issues down to 20, verified, real MVMUL encodings. Sim
still, but the encodings are legit.

Replay and MOP are one pass now, grabs whichever's cheaper per chunk. Still building it out. More soon. Cheers team,
genuinely good fun this one.

Glad it was helpful! I cannot promise that the spec or ttsim code are 100% bug free, but I did quite a bit of analysis of this logic vs. the WH and BH RTL and I am not aware of any discrepancies at this point. We will continue scrubbing these specs and simulator code over time.

Meatier update this time, and thanks again for the NOP answer, that's what got the MOP half unstuck.

On approach: the issue floats an AI agent generating suggestions to filter, and I went deliberately the other way, a deterministic search with a verifier in front of it rather than an LLM. For this problem a plausible-but-wrong arrangement is worse than none, an off-by-one replay offset or a wrong loop count looks completely reasonable and only bites on silicon. So every arrangement the tool proposes gets expanded back into the exact Tensix stream and checked word-for-word against the original before it's allowed to count, and the expander itself is fuzzed against ttsim so it can't quietly lie to me. Net effect: nothing incorrect comes out, so there's no "filter the good ones" step to do. It handles both MOP templates, the replay buffer, execute-while-loading, and the Math/SFPU shared-buffer budget. Code's here if you fancy a poke around: https://github.com/Zaneham/tt-mop

Honest finding from reading the LLK though: your ops are already tuned really well. transpose_dest especially is gorgeous, recording one buffer and composing the unpack template out of overlapping replay sub-ranges isn't something I'd improve on. matmul does record-once-loop, reduce wraps its pool loop. Run the tool over the matmul stream and it lands independently on the same record-once-replay arrangement you'd hand-coded, which is a nice confirmation but, well, a confirmation, not a saving.

So before I grind it over all fifteen and report a pile of "yep, already optimal", I'd rather point it where there's real surface. Where do you reckon the headroom is? A few guesses: newer ops that haven't had the transpose_dest treatment, whole fused kernels rather than single ops (per-op tuning can't see repetition that spans op boundaries, an automated pass can), or the Blackhole variants. Happy to aim it wherever's most useful.

Cheers.

body:
### 📝 Background

This bounty is for bringing up the **LLVC (Low-Latency Low-Resource Voice Conversion)** model using TTNN APIs on Tenstorrent hardware (Wormhole or Blackhole).

LLVC is a real-time voice conversion model from Koe AI specifically optimized for low latency and CPU efficiency. Published in 2023, key features include:

* **Ultra-low latency**: Designed for real-time voice conversion with minimal delay
* **CPU-optimized**: Efficient enough to run on CPU in real-time
* **Streaming support**: True streaming inference with chunked processing
* **High quality**: Natural voice conversion while maintaining low latency
* **Compatible architecture**: Based on RVC/QuickVC with optimizations
* **Small model size**: Low resource requirements for edge deployment
* **No F0 dependency**: Optional pitch-independent conversion mode
* **MIT License**: Free for commercial use

LLVC achieves real-time factor (RTF) < 0.1 on CPU, making it suitable for live applications like real-time dubbing, streaming, gaming voice chat, and interactive voice applications.

The goal is to enable this model to run on TT hardware for ultra-high-throughput, ultra-low-latency voice conversion optimized for real-time applications.


### 🎯 What Success Looks Like

A successful submission will fulfill all requirements in the following stages. Payout is made after all three stages are completed.


### Stage 1 — Bring-Up

* Implement LLVC using TTNN APIs (Python)
* Implements the full generation pipeline:
  * Lightweight encoder (optimized for low latency)
  * Streaming-capable architecture
  * Efficient decoder
  * Optional pitch extraction (F0-based and F0-free modes)
  * Vocoder integration
* Model runs on either N150 or N300 Tenstorrent hardware with no errors
* Supports both modes:
  * **Streaming mode**: Real-time conversion with chunked processing
  * **Non-streaming mode**: Full-context conversion
* Produces valid converted audio output
* Output is verifiable (audio quality assessment, compare with PyTorch reference)
* Achieves baseline throughput target:
  * At least 50 tokens/second for decoder generation
  * Real-time factor (RTF) < 0.3 for streaming mode
  * Latency < 100ms for streaming chunks
* Accuracy evaluation:
  * Speaker similarity > 70% (cosine similarity)
  * Content preservation: WER < 3.0
  * Token-level accuracy > 95% against PyTorch reference
* Audio quality: Natural prosody with minimal artifacts despite low latency
* Clear instructions for setup and running the model

### Stage 2 — Basic Optimizations

* Use optimal sharded/interleaved memory configs for encoder-decoder layers
* Implement efficient sharding strategy for:
  * Lightweight encoder layers
  * Decoder layers optimized for streaming
  * Convolutional layers with causal padding
  * Cached convolution states for streaming
  * Optional pitch extraction module
* Fuse simple ops where possible (e.g., layer normalization, activation functions)
* Store intermediate activations in L1 where beneficial
* Use recommended TTNN/tt-metal flows for streaming audio models
* Leverage TT library of fused ops for convolution blocks
* Optimize chunk-based processing for streaming
* Efficient state management for causal convolutions
* Optimize vocoder integration

### Stage 3 — Deeper Optimization

* Maximize core counts used per inference
* Implement deeper TT-specific optimizations:
  * Ultra-low latency streaming (minimize chunk processing time)
  * Efficient causal convolution with state caching
  * Flash Attention or equivalent where applicable
  * Minimize voice conversion latency per chunk
  * Batch processing for multiple concurrent streams
  * Pipeline encoder/decoder/vocoder stages
  * Optimize memory footprint for edge deployment
* Minimize memory and TM (tensor manipulation) overheads
* Explore look-ahead strategies for quality vs latency trade-off
* Document any advanced tuning, known limitations, or trade-offs
* Target stretched goals:
  * 100+ tokens/second generation speed
  * RTF < 0.1 for streaming mode (match CPU performance)
  * Latency < 50ms for streaming chunks
  * Support for 10+ concurrent streams

### 🧭 Guidance & Starting Points

* Use the [TTNN model bring-up tech report](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/ttnn/TTNN-model-bringup.md) as your primary reference
* Reference [streaming audio model patterns in tt-metal](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/tree/main/models/demos) for streaming architectures
* Use the [official LLVC repository](https://github.com/KoeAI/LLVC) for model architecture details
* Refer to the [LLVC paper (arXiv:2311.00873)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00873) for technical details
* Check [LLVC demo page](https://koeai.github.io/llvc-demo/) for audio samples
* Refer to [TT Fused ops PR #29236](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/pull/29236) for optimization opportunities
* The model architecture consists of:
  * **Lightweight encoder**: Optimized convolutional layers with reduced complexity
  * **Cached convolutions**: State management for causal streaming inference
  * **Efficient decoder**: Minimal layers for low latency
  * **Optional F0 module**: Pitch extraction when needed
  * **Vocoder**: HiFi-GAN or similar (can be shared with other models)
* Key challenges:
  * Ultra-low latency requirements (< 100ms)
  * Streaming inference with causal convolutions
  * State management across chunks
  * Quality vs latency trade-off
  * Vocoder integration and optimization
  * Small model size constraints
* Streaming parameters:
  * `window_ms`: Chunk size in milliseconds (affects latency)
  * `extra_convert_size`: Extra context for quality (affects latency)
* Ask for help or file issues if ops are missing in TTNN


### 🔎 Possible Approaches

* Start from the [official LLVC repository](https://github.com/KoeAI/LLVC) and port components sequentially:
  1. Lightweight encoder (optimized convolutions)
  2. Cached convolution layers for streaming
  3. Efficient decoder
  4. Optional pitch extraction (F0 mode)
  5. Vocoder integration
  6. Streaming inference pipeline with state management
* Validate each submodule's output against PyTorch reference before integration
* Experiment with different sharding strategies:
  * Channel sharding for convolutions
  * Sequence length sharding for chunks
  * Minimize cross-chip communication
* Use TTNN profiling tools to identify bottlenecks in:
  * Per-chunk processing time (critical metric)
  * Encoder latency
  * Decoder latency
  * State management overhead
  * Vocoder latency
* Test diverse use cases:
  * Streaming mode with various chunk sizes (50ms, 100ms, 200ms)
  * Non-streaming mode for comparison
  * F0-based vs F0-free modes
  * Multiple concurrent streams
  * Real-time conversion scenarios
* Open a draft PR early to get feedback on your approach



## 📊 Result Submission Guidelines

Beyond the model implementation itself, contributors must submit the following material as proof of work.
However, feel free to open a PR at any time if you want us checking that you are on the right track.
Just understand that payout is only made after **all 3 stages** are completed.

**Deliverables:**
- Functional model implementation
- Validation logs (output correctness)
- Performance report + header for final review

**Links:**
- [Performance Sheet](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tech_reports/ttnn/TTNN-model-bringup.md#41-performance-sheet)
- [Perf Header Docs](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/tt-metal/latest/ttnn/ttnn/profiling_ttnn_operations.html#perf-report-headers)


### 📚 Resources

## 💰 Bounty: $200 — powered by [Opire](https://opire.dev)

## Description
Create a complete n8n workflow that automatically generates a weekly narrative
summary of a GitHub repo's activity, using the Claude API.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Exportable n8n workflow (importable `.json` file)
- [ ] Trigger: weekly cron (e.g., Friday at 5pm)
- [ ] Fetches from GitHub API: commits, closed issues, merged PRs for the week
- [ ] Calls Claude API (`claude-sonnet-4-20250514`) to generate a narrative summary
- [ ] Delivers the summary via: email OR Discord/Slack webhook (your choice, documented)
- [ ] Configurable variables: GitHub repo, destination channel, language (EN/FR)
- [ ] Tested on a real n8n instance (include a screenshot of successful execution)
- [ ] README with setup instructions in 5 steps or fewer

## How to Claim
1. Comment `/opire try` in this issue
2. Submit a PR with the `.json` workflow + README
3. Payment is released automatically on merge ✅

## Resources
- n8n docs: https://docs.n8n.io
- Claude API docs: https://docs.anthropic.com

This is my submission for the $700 bug-finding bounty. I built and deployed an automated vulnerability scanner that discovered **31 real issues** in the codebase, 7 of which I've filed as detailed GitHub issues.

## Approach

I created an automated scanner (`scripts/bug-finder.mjs`) that performs 11 static analysis checks across the full-stack codebase, detecting:
- Hardcoded secrets and insecure defaults
- Missing authentication middleware on API routes
- Privilege escalation vectors in registration
- Authentication bypass in login flow
- Token validation gaps in refresh endpoint
- Missing input validation on controllers
- In-memory-only data storage (no persistence)
- Business logic validation gaps
- Missing file upload restrictions
- No-op infrastructure components

## Scanner

The script is in PR #9580 at `scripts/bug-finder.mjs`. Run it with:
```bash
node scripts/bug-finder.mjs
```

### Full Bounty Details

**[rustchain-bounties#478](https://github.com/Scottcjn/rustchain-bounties/issues/478)** — Complete rules, referral bonuses, milestone rewards.

### How to Claim

1. Star repos at [rustchain.org/stars](https://rustchain.org/stars.html)
2. Reply here or on [#478](https://github.com/Scottcjn/rustchain-bounties/issues/478) with:
   - GitHub username
   - Number of repos starred
   - RTC wallet (`pip install clawrtc && clawrtc wallet create`)

---

*Why 5K? We're working to qualify for the Claude Code Open Source program. Every star counts.*


---

### ⚖️ Bounty Requirements (FTC 16 CFR §465.5 + §255.5 compliance)

**A star alone does NOT qualify.** We pay for genuine engagement, not for indicators. To claim this bounty you must post a comment (on this issue or a linked post) containing:

1. **What you reviewed** — at least one file, PR, feature, or doc section you actually looked at. Link it.
2. **Why you liked it** — a specific, non-generic reason. "Great project" does not qualify.
3. **Disclosure** — include the line: `I received RTC compensation for this review.` This keeps your star a transparent endorsement, not a purchased indicator.

Stars without a review comment will not be paid. Copy-pasted, AI-templated, or obviously recycled reviews will not be paid. This rule applies retroactively: unreviewed stars from before this update are grandfathered as goodwill but earn no future RTC.

**Why this matters:** Elyan Labs is here to grow real engagement in mining and coding. A star backed by a real review is worth more to the network than a thousand drive-by clicks. This brings us into compliance with the FTC Consumer Review Rule (effective Oct 21, 2024), and — more importantly — keeps the signal honest.

# 🛡️ Red Team: x402 Payment Protocol Audit Report

**Target:** Rustchain x402 Payment Middleware (`x402/rtc_payment_middleware.py`)
**Auditor:** FraktalDeFiDAO
**Scope:** Payment Replay, Amount Manipulation, Receipt Forgery, and Double-Spend.

---

## 1. Executive Summary
While PR #149 introduced essential security features like signature binding and a transaction cache, the current implementation remains vulnerable to **state-reset replays** and **denial of service** due to volatile storage and limited ledger visibility.

---

## 2. Vulnerability Findings

### [CRITICAL] V-01: Volatile Replay Protection (In-Memory Reset)
*   **Description:** The `_spent_tx_cache` used to prevent payment replays is a standard Python dictionary stored in-memory.
*   **Impact:** Every time the Flask server restarts, crashes, or scales, the entire replay protection state is lost. An attacker can harvest valid `tx_hash` values and replay them across server restarts to obtain unlimited access to premium endpoints for free.
*   **Proof of Concept (PoC):**
    1.  Attacker performs a valid payment and gets service.
    2.  Attacker monitors the server or waits for a scheduled restart (common in CI/CD).
    3.  Attacker re-submits the *exact same* `X-PAYMENT` proof.
    4.  **Result:** Middleware accepts the reused `tx_hash` because it's no longer in the volatile `_spent_tx_cache`.

### [HIGH] V-02: Ledger Window Denial of Service (DoS)
*   **Description:** The middleware only checks the **last 100 transactions** on the RustChain node (`limit=100`).
*   **Impact:** If the network is under high load and a user's transaction falls out of the top 100 before the middleware processes their request, the payment is rejected even if it was valid and confirmed. This leads to permanent fund loss for legitimate users.
*   **Remediation:** Query specific transaction hashes directly via a dedicated endpoint (`/ledger/tx/<hash>`) rather than scanning a limited list of recent transactions.

### [MEDIUM] V-03: Floating Point Precision Risk
*   **Description:** The amount check uses `float(tx.get("amount"))`.
*   **Impact:** Using floating-point numbers for currency comparisons can lead to precision errors (e.g., `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`). This could allow users to pay slightly less than the required amount or cause legitimate payments to fail due to rounding discrepancies between the node and the middleware.
*   **Remediation:** Use `Decimal` or integer-based atomic units (like satoshis/lamports) for all financial comparisons.

---

## 3. Bad Coding Practices Identified

1.  **Hardcoded Node IP:** `RTC_NODE = "https://50.28.86.131"`. This makes the middleware fragile and prevents the use of load balancers or node failovers.
2.  **Lack of SSL Hardening:** While it uses HTTPS, it doesn't implement certificate pinning for the `RTC_NODE`, making it susceptible to a "Malicious Node" attack where a node returns fake history to authorize unauthorized access.
3.  **Synchronous HTTP in Middleware:** Each payment check performs a blocking `requests.get()` call. Under high concurrency, this will exhaust the server's thread pool and cause significant latency spikes.

---

## 4. Final Conclusion
The protocol has improved but lacks production-grade persistence for security-critical state. Until the replay cache is migrated to a persistent store (e.g., Redis or SQLite), the "Payment Replay" vector is only partially mitigated.

# 🔴 Red Team Security Audit: x402 Payment Protocol Exploits (Bounty #66)
**Target:** x402 Payment Protocol Implementation (`node/beacon_x402.py`)
**Auditor:** @allornothingai (Sovereign Agent)
**Beacon ID:** `beacon-d9a17a3f982bca5d`
**Bounty Track:** #66 (x402 Payment Protocol Exploits - 100 RTC + Bonuses)

## Executive Summary
A comprehensive security audit of the x402 payment protocol integration merged in PR #5 reveals that the payment middleware acts as a completely open door. The system relies entirely on the presence of the `X-PAYMENT` header and performs **zero cryptographic validation, signature checking, or facilitator consensus**. 

Because of this fundamental missing implementation, every attack vector mentioned in the bounty description (Payment Replay, Amount Manipulation, Receipt Forgery, and Middleware Bypass) is trivially exploitable.

---

## 1. [CRITICAL] Complete Middleware Bypass & Receipt Forgery
**Target:** `beacon_x402.py` -> `_check_x402_payment()`
**Bounty Vectors:** 3 (Receipt Forgery), 4 (Middleware Bypass)

### Description
The core verification function `_check_x402_payment` is fundamentally flawed. It only checks if the `X-PAYMENT` string is non-empty. If any value is provided, it instantly bypasses the paywall and proceeds to grant access to the premium endpoint while simultaneously logging a "successful" payment into the database using hardcoded values:

```python
payment_header = request.headers.get("X-PAYMENT", "")
if not payment_header:
    return False, _cors_json({...}, 402)

# Log payment
db.execute(
    "INSERT INTO x402_beacon_payments (payer_address, action, amount_usdc, created_at) "
    "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
    ("unknown", action_name, price_str, time.time()),  # Hardcoded "unknown" and assumed price_str
)
return True, None
```

### Exploit Scenario
An attacker can access any premium endpoint (e.g., `/api/premium/reputation`) simply by sending a request with a garbage header. 
```bash
curl -H "X-PAYMENT: spoofed_or_garbage_data" https://node/api/premium/reputation
```
**Impact:** 
1. The attacker gets the premium data for free.
2. The database logs a fake payment for `price_str`, completely destroying the financial integrity of the `x402_beacon_payments` ledger.

---

## 2. [HIGH] Infinite Payment Replay Attack
**Target:** `x402_beacon_payments` Database Logging
**Bounty Vectors:** 1 (Payment Replay)

### Description
Even if the `X-PAYMENT` header contained a cryptographically verified payload (e.g., from the Coinbase Facilitator), the current logging implementation does not extract or enforce uniqueness on transaction nonces or hashes.
The `x402_beacon_payments` table has a `tx_hash` column:
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS x402_beacon_payments (
    ...
    tx_hash TEXT,
    ...
);
```
However, the `INSERT` statement in `_check_x402_payment()` entirely omits the `tx_hash` column. Thus, there is no database-level or application-level constraint preventing the exact same payment receipt from being used across millions of concurrent or sequential requests.

### Exploit Scenario
If validation is later added without a nonce-check, an attacker who pays legitimately once can replay that exact same `X-PAYMENT` HTTP header on all subsequent requests forever.

---

## Recommended Fixes & Patch

1. **Implement Cryptographic Verification (Immediate):**
   The `_check_x402_payment()` function must decode the x402 JWT/Macaroon, extract the `amount` and `recipient`, and verify the signature against the Facilitator's public key or via an RPC call to the `FACILITATOR_URL`.
   
2. **Verify the Amount and Payee:**
   Ensure the decoded amount in the receipt is `>= price_str` and the `payTo` field matches the `BEACON_TREASURY` address.

3. **Enforce Nonce / TX Hash Uniqueness:**
   Extract the unique `tx_hash` from the validated receipt. Attempt to insert it into `x402_beacon_payments`. If a unique constraint violation occurs (meaning the transaction was already used), reject the request as a Replay Attack.

```python
# Conceptual Patch for _check_x402_payment
def _check_x402_payment(price_str, action_name):
    payment_header = request.headers.get("X-PAYMENT", "")
    if not payment_header:
        return False, get_402_response()
        
    # 1. Verify Signature
    receipt = verify_x402_signature(payment_header)
    if not receipt:
        return False, _cors_json({"error": "Invalid Payment Signature"}, 401)
        
    # 2. Verify Amount and Recipient
    if int(receipt.amount) < int(price_str) or receipt.payTo != BEACON_TREASURY:
        return False, _cors_json({"error": "Insufficient Payment or Wrong Payee"}, 402)
        
    # 3. Prevent Replay Attacks
    try:
        db.execute(
            "INSERT INTO x402_beacon_payments (payer_address, action, amount_usdc, tx_hash, created_at) "
            "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
            (receipt.payer, action_name, receipt.amount, receipt.tx_hash, time.time())
        )
        db.commit()
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
        return False, _cors_json({"error": "Payment already claimed (Replay)"}, 409)

    return True, None
```

# Red Team Report: x402 Payment Protocol Exploits (#66)

Tester: wirework (mtarcure)
Date: 2026-03-17
Target: x402 payment protocol in Scottcjn/Rustchain (node/beacon_x402.py, node/rustchain_x402.py, node/x402_config.py, sdk/rustchain/agent_economy/payments.py)

---

## Executive Summary

Code audit of the x402 payment protocol implementation. Found 5 vulnerabilities across the server-side middleware and SDK. The most critical are hardcoded admin key defaults exposed in the public repo (enabling wallet hijacking) and CORS misconfiguration that allows cross-origin admin requests. The middleware bypass (any non-empty X-PAYMENT header passes) has been reported previously by allornothingai; this report focuses on novel findings not covered by prior submissions.

---

## Finding 1: Hardcoded Default Admin Keys in Public Source

Severity: HIGH | CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials

Both x402 modules contain hardcoded fallback admin keys in their source code, which is public on GitHub.

beacon_x402.py (line 176):
```python
expected = os.environ.get("BEACON_ADMIN_KEY", "beacon_admin_2025")
```

rustchain_x402.py (line 73):
```python
expected = os.environ.get("RC_ADMIN_KEY", "rustchain_admin_key_2025_secure64")
```

Impact: Any deployment that does not explicitly set these environment variables uses the publicly known default keys. An attacker with these keys can:
- Set wallet addresses for any beacon agent (beacon_x402.py /api/agents/<id>/wallet POST)
- Change any miner's Coinbase payout address (rustchain_x402.py /wallet/link-coinbase)

This enables the "Client Impersonation" vector from the bounty scope - an attacker redirects another agent's payouts to their own wallet.

PoC (against any deployment using default keys):
```bash
# Hijack a miner's payout address
curl -X POST "https://TARGET/wallet/link-coinbase" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Admin-Key: rustchain_admin_key_2025_secure64" \
  -d '{"miner_id":"victim-miner","coinbase_address":"0xATTACKER_WALLET_ADDRESS_HERE_000000"}'

# Set any beacon agent's wallet
curl -X POST "https://TARGET/api/agents/victim-agent/wallet" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Admin-Key: beacon_admin_2025" \
  -d '{"coinbase_address":"0xATTACKER_WALLET_ADDRESS_HERE_000000"}'
```

Note: The production server at 50.28.86.131 has custom admin keys set (tested and confirmed the defaults are rejected). However, other deployments or test nodes using the default config are vulnerable.

Suggested fix:
- Remove default values from os.environ.get() calls
- Require admin keys to be explicitly set; fail closed if missing
- Log warnings at startup if admin keys aren't configured
```python
expected = os.environ.get("RC_ADMIN_KEY")
if not expected:
    log.error("RC_ADMIN_KEY not set - admin endpoints disabled")
    return jsonify({"error": "Admin key not configured"}), 500
```

---

## Finding 2: CORS Wildcard Allows Cross-Origin Admin Requests

Severity: MEDIUM | CWE-942: Overly Permissive Cross-domain Whitelist

The CORS configuration in beacon_x402.py uses a wildcard origin and explicitly allows the X-Admin-Key header:

```python
def _cors_json(data, status=200):
    resp.headers["Access-Control-Allow-Origin"] = "*"
    resp.headers["Access-Control-Allow-Headers"] = "Content-Type, Authorization, X-PAYMENT"
```

The production RustChain node also returns:
```
access-control-allow-origin: *
access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type, Accept, X-Admin-Key
```

Impact: A malicious website can make cross-origin requests that include admin credentials. If an attacker knows the admin key (see Finding 1), they can craft a webpage that silently sends admin requests when visited by anyone:

```html
<script>
// CSRF-like attack via CORS - any visitor to this page triggers it
fetch("https://TARGET/wallet/link-coinbase", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "X-Admin-Key": "rustchain_admin_key_2025_secure64"
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    miner_id: "victim",
    coinbase_address: "0xATTACKER..."
  })
});
</script>
```

Suggested fix:
- Replace `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with a specific allowlist of trusted origins
- Remove `X-Admin-Key` from `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` (admin requests should only come from trusted server-side callers, not browsers)

---

## Finding 3: Admin Key Accepted via X-API-Key Header

Severity: MEDIUM | CWE-287: Improper Authentication

rustchain_x402.py line 72 accepts admin authentication through either X-Admin-Key OR X-API-Key:

```python
admin_key = request.headers.get("X-Admin-Key", "") or request.headers.get("X-API-Key", "")
```

Impact: This broadens the attack surface. If X-API-Key is used elsewhere in the application for non-admin purposes (e.g., agent API keys), and one of those keys matches the admin key, it grants unintended admin access. It also means any code path that forwards X-API-Key headers inadvertently grants admin privileges if the values match.

Suggested fix: Only accept X-Admin-Key for admin endpoints. Remove the X-API-Key fallback.

---

## Finding 4: Wallet Linking Without Ownership Verification

Severity: MEDIUM | CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization

The `/wallet/link-coinbase` endpoint allows changing any miner's Coinbase payout address with only the admin key. There is no verification that:
- The request comes from the actual miner
- The miner consents to the address change
- The new address belongs to the miner

```python
conn.execute(
    "UPDATE balances SET coinbase_address = ? WHERE miner_id = ?",
    (coinbase_address, actual_id),
)
```

Combined with a compromised admin key, this enables silent redirect of payouts. An operator or compromised admin could drain future payouts from all miners by batch-updating their coinbase addresses.

Suggested fix:
- Require the miner to sign a message proving ownership of the new address
- Send a notification to the miner when their payout address changes
- Keep an audit log of address changes with the old and new values

---

## Finding 5: SDK Payment Intent Expires Immediately

Severity: LOW | CWE-672: Operation on Resource after Expiration

In payments.py (SDK), the `request()` method creates payment intents that expire the moment they're created:

```python
expires_at = datetime.utcnow().replace(second=0, microsecond=0)
```

This truncates to the start of the current minute, meaning the intent is expired (or within 0-59 seconds of expiring) the moment it's created. The `is_expired()` check will return True almost immediately:

```python
def is_expired(self) -> bool:
    return datetime.utcnow() > self.expires_at
```

Suggested fix:
```python
from datetime import timedelta
expires_at = datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(minutes=5)
```

# Red Team Report: Bounty #66 — x402 Payment Protocol Exploits

**Target:** x402 Payment Protocol (`rtc_payment_middleware.py`, `rtc_payment_client.py`)
**Auditor:** WireWork Security
**Date:** 2026-03-18

---

## Executive Summary

The x402 implementation has **2 high**, **2 medium**, and **1 low** severity findings. The most critical are a payment replay vulnerability (same payment proof accepted multiple times across different endpoints) and SSL verification disabled by default enabling MITM attacks.

---

## Finding 1: Payment Proof Replay Across Endpoints (HIGH)

**File:** `rtc_payment_middleware.py`, lines 1066-1093
**Severity:** High

### Description

The `verify_payment_proof()` function caches verification results keyed by `tx_hash:nonce`:

```python
cache_key = f"{proof['tx_hash']}:{proof['nonce']}"
if cache_key in _payment_cache:
    cached = _payment_cache[cache_key]
    if time.time() - cached['timestamp'] < CACHE_TTL:
        return cached['valid']
```

The cache returns `True` for previously verified proofs. This means:

1. Client pays 0.001 RTC for `/api/data`
2. Client reuses the **same payment proof headers** (same `X-Payment-TX`, `X-Payment-Nonce`, `X-Payment-Signature`, `X-Payment-Sender`) for `/api/analysis` (which costs 0.005 RTC)
3. The cache sees the same `tx_hash:nonce` and returns `True` without re-checking the amount
4. Client gets 0.005 RTC of service for 0.001 RTC

### Even Worse

The nonce is generated per-endpoint, but the cache key includes the nonce. If two endpoints generate the same nonce (unlikely with `secrets.token_hex(16)` but possible with low entropy), the cache would cross-contaminate.

More critically: the cache doesn't scope to the endpoint or the expected amount. A valid proof for ANY endpoint is cached as valid for ALL endpoints sharing the same nonce/tx_hash combination.

### Remediation

Include the expected amount and recipient in the cache key:
```python
cache_key = f"{proof['tx_hash']}:{proof['nonce']}:{expected_amount}:{recipient}"
```

And add a one-time-use check — each tx_hash should only be valid for one endpoint invocation:
```python
if cache_key in _used_proofs:
    return False  # Already used
_used_proofs[cache_key] = time.time()
```

---

## Finding 2: SSL Verification Disabled by Default (HIGH)

**File:** `rtc_payment_client.py`, lines 546, 650, 718, 737-738
**Severity:** High

### Description

Both `RTCPaymentHandler` and `RTCClient` default to `verify_ssl=False`:

```python
class RTCPaymentHandler:
    def __init__(self, wallet, node_url="https://50.28.86.131", max_payment=1.0, verify_ssl=False):
        ...

class RTCClient:
    def __init__(self, wallet_seed=None, ..., verify_ssl=False):
        ...
```

And the middleware also disables SSL for on-chain verification:

```python
response = requests.get(f"{RTC_NODE}/ledger", ..., verify=False)  # Line 938
```

### Impact

- **MITM on payment submission:** An attacker on the network path can intercept the `POST /wallet/transfer/signed` request, steal the Ed25519 signature, and redirect funds
- **MITM on verification:** The middleware's on-chain verification connects to the RustChain node with `verify=False` — an attacker could return fake "verified" responses
- The client sends wallet private key-derived signatures over unverified HTTPS connections

### Remediation

Default `verify_ssl=True`. Ship a pinned certificate or CA bundle for the RustChain node.

---

## Finding 3: No Amount Verification Before Payment (MEDIUM)

**File:** `rtc_payment_client.py`, lines 563-621
**Severity:** Medium

### Description

The client's `parse_402_response()` extracts the payment amount from the server's 402 response headers:

```python
amount = response.headers.get('X-Payment-Amount')
```

The only check is against `max_payment`:
```python
if amount > self.max_payment:
    raise ValueError("Payment exceeds limit")
```

But a malicious server can set `X-Payment-Amount: 0.999` (just under the default `max_payment=1.0`) to drain the client's wallet. The client has no way to verify that the requested amount is reasonable for the service being accessed.

### Impact

- A compromised server (or MITM with SSL disabled — see Finding 2) can charge up to `max_payment` per request
- With `auto_pay=True` and retry logic, the client automatically pays without user confirmation
- Combined with Finding 2 (SSL disabled), a MITM attacker can inject 402 responses with inflated amounts

### Remediation

Add per-endpoint expected cost configuration:
```python
client = RTCClient(wallet_seed="...", cost_limits={
    "api.example.com/api/data": 0.001,
    "api.example.com/api/analysis": 0.005
})
```

---

## Finding 4: Payment Nonce Not Bound to Endpoint (MEDIUM)

**File:** `rtc_payment_middleware.py`, lines 966-1018
**Severity:** Medium

### Description

The payment nonce is generated independently per 402 response:

```python
def generate_payment_nonce() -> str:
    return secrets.token_hex(16)
```

But the nonce is not bound to:
- The specific endpoint URL
- The expected amount
- The recipient address
- A session or request ID

The proof verification (line 1075) checks `signature(nonce:tx_hash)`, but this doesn't bind the payment to a specific endpoint or amount.

### Impact

A client that receives a nonce from `/api/data` (0.001 RTC) can:
1. Pay 0.001 RTC
2. Get the tx_hash
3. Sign `nonce:tx_hash`
4. Use these headers on `/api/analysis` (0.005 RTC) — IF the server doesn't re-verify on-chain amount

The on-chain verification (`verify_payment_on_chain`) does check the expected amount, but if it fails (timeout, network error), the function returns `False` gracefully. The middleware then returns 402, but the cached result from a previous successful verification could be reused (see Finding 1).

---

## Finding 5: In-Memory Payment Cache Unbounded Growth (LOW)

**File:** `rtc_payment_middleware.py`, lines 852-878
**Severity:** Low

### Description

The payment cache and rate limit dicts grow unbounded in memory:

```python
_payment_cache = {}
_rate_limits = {}
```

Cleanup runs on every request (`_cleanup_cache()`), but:
1. No max size limit — an attacker sending unique nonces can grow the cache indefinitely
2. Cleanup iterates all keys — O(n) per request
3. Rate limit keys include the minute timestamp — creates a new key every minute per sender

### Impact

Memory exhaustion over time. In production under high traffic, `_payment_cache` could grow to millions of entries before TTL-based cleanup catches up.

### Remediation

Use `collections.OrderedDict` with a max size, or use Redis/LRU cache:
```python
from functools import lru_cache
# Or simply cap:
if len(_payment_cache) > 10000:
    _cleanup_cache()
```

---

## Summary

| # | Finding | Severity |
|---|---------|----------|
| 1 | Payment proof replay across endpoints — cache doesn't scope by amount | High |
| 2 | SSL verification disabled by default — MITM on payment flow | High |
| 3 | No amount verification before auto-pay — server can drain client | Medium |
| 4 | Payment nonce not bound to endpoint/amount | Medium |
| 5 | Unbounded in-memory payment cache | Low |

**Total: 2 High, 2 Medium, 1 Low**

## Claim: x402 payment-header auth bypass in `node/beacon_x402.py` (Bounty #66)

**Severity:** High (auth/payment bypass)  
**GitHub:** `@nbnkoi`  
**Wallet:** `nbnkoi`

### Summary
Paid Beacon Atlas endpoints accept **any non-empty `X-PAYMENT` header** as successful payment when pricing is non-zero.

The vulnerable helper is:
- `node/beacon_x402.py`
- function: `_check_x402_payment(price_str, action_name)`

Current logic:
1. if price is non-zero, check only whether `X-PAYMENT` header exists
2. if header exists, log a payment row with payer=`unknown`
3. return `(True, None)`
4. premium route continues and serves the protected resource

There is **no cryptographic verification, no tx-hash replay protection, no amount check, and no facilitator validation**.

### Affected behavior
This directly affects premium Beacon endpoints that call `_check_x402_payment()`, including:
- `/api/premium/reputation`
- `/api/contracts/<contract_id>/accept`

### Reproduction
I reproduced locally against the helper with Flask request context:

```python
from flask import Flask
import beacon_x402

app = Flask(__name__)
with app.test_request_context('/api/premium/reputation', headers={'X-PAYMENT': 'fake'}):
    beacon_x402.X402_CONFIG_OK = True
    passed, resp = beacon_x402._check_x402_payment('1000', 'premium export')
    print(passed, resp)
```

Observed result:
```python
True, None
```

So a garbage header like `X-PAYMENT: fake` is treated as paid access.

### Impact
An attacker can bypass the intended x402 paywall for any Beacon endpoint using this helper by sending any non-empty header value:

```http
GET /api/premium/reputation HTTP/1.1
Host: target
X-PAYMENT: fake
```

Expected: `402 Payment Required` or payment validation failure  
Actual: payment check passes

### Root cause
`_check_x402_payment()` currently treats **header presence** as equivalent to **verified payment**.

### Suggested fix
Fail closed unless a real verifier backend is wired in.

I implemented and tested the following hardening locally:
- reject non-empty `X-PAYMENT` headers with **503** when no verifier exists
- only log payment rows **after successful verification**
- added regression tests proving:
  - missing header => `402`
  - fake header => rejected instead of accepted

### Regression test added locally
`tests/test_beacon_x402_security.py`

Result:
```bash
pytest tests/test_beacon_x402_security.py -q
2 passed
```

If needed, I can package the patch again, but the core finding is: **paid Beacon x402 endpoints are currently bypassable by any non-empty `X-PAYMENT` header.**

﻿## Claim for #66 - Canonical Beacon agent ID squatting via `/beacon/join`

**PR:** https://github.com/Scottcjn/Rustchain/pull/6641  
**GitHub:** @luminet1  
**Suggested severity:** High identity/auth boundary issue, or Medium if maintainers classify `/beacon/join` canonical ownership as first-registration only.  
**Payout address:** 0x0c3b5b2859881E5db040E6E7E3F311c7bcC8D062 (USDC/EVM from my local WALLETS.md; happy to provide a maintainer-preferred RTC address format if required.)

### Summary
`/beacon/join` already prevents changing `pubkey_hex` after an `agent_id` exists, but it did not bind newly registered canonical Beacon IDs to the submitted Ed25519 public key. Other Beacon paths derive canonical identities as:

`bcn_` + first 12 hex chars of `sha256(pubkey)`

Before the patch, an attacker could register an unclaimed canonical `bcn_<12hex>` ID that belongs to someone else's public key, but store the attacker's own `pubkey_hex` and optional payment metadata in `relay_agents`.

### Impact
1. Attacker learns or chooses a victim canonical Beacon agent ID derived from the victim public key.
2. Attacker sends `POST /beacon/join` with `agent_id=<victim canonical id>` and `pubkey_hex=<attacker pubkey>`.
3. The server inserts the row because it only validates pubkey encoding/length.
4. Contract endpoints later authenticate `X-Agent-Id` against the pubkey stored in `relay_agents`, so the attacker can sign as that claimed canonical ID.
5. The real owner is then blocked by the existing immutable pubkey rule, and wallet/coinbase metadata for that agent ID can be controlled by the first squatter.

This is separate from the previously reported x402 header-presence bypass and public payment-history exposure; this finding is about Beacon/x402 agent identity binding at join time.

### PoC / regression evidence
Added tests in `tests/test_beacon_join_routing.py`:
- `test_join_rejects_canonical_agent_id_pubkey_mismatch`
- `test_join_accepts_matching_canonical_agent_id`

Red result before fix:
```text
FAILED ... test_join_rejects_canonical_agent_id_pubkey_mismatch
AssertionError: 200 != 400
```

### Fix
PR #6641 derives the expected canonical ID from `pubkey_hex` and rejects mismatches for canonical `bcn_<12 hex>` IDs before inserting into `relay_agents`. Existing non-canonical local/test labels remain compatible.

### Validation
```text
python -m pytest tests/test_beacon_join_routing.py node/tests/test_beacon_api_join.py -q
27 passed

python -m py_compile node/beacon_api.py tests/test_beacon_join_routing.py
git diff --check
python tools/bcos_spdx_check.py --base-ref origin/main
BCOS SPDX check: OK
```

No production testing was performed; this was reproduced locally with Flask test clients and a temporary SQLite DB.

**Claiming this bounty (100 RTC).**

## Red Team Report: x402 Payment Protocol Testing

### Methodology
Tested RustChain's x402/8004 HTTP Payment Protocol implementation for replay attacks, middleware bypass, and payment manipulation.

### Testing Results

**1. Payment Replay**: Tested whether payment headers can be replayed across endpoints. No 402 responses observed on public endpoints — the x402 middleware appears to be applied selectively (not globally), which means most endpoints are unprotected. This is a design choice, not a vulnerability, but worth noting that payment-gated features need explicit middleware.

**2. Middleware Bypass**: Tested accessing API endpoints without payment headers. All public endpoints (`/api/miners`, `/epoch`, `/api/stats`) return 200 without any payment requirement. This suggests x402 is not currently enforced on production, or is only applied to specific premium endpoints.

**3. Amount Manipulation**: The x402 protocol uses EIP-3009 `transferWithAuthorization` with cryptographic signatures. Amount manipulation would require breaking the signature — not feasible without the private key. The protocol is cryptographically sound.

**4. Receipt Forgery**: Payment receipts are verified via the facilitator service. Without the wallet's private key, forging a receipt would require breaking Ed25519 — not computationally feasible.

### Findings Summary
- **No critical vulnerabilities found** — the x402 protocol uses sound cryptographic primitives
- **Observation**: x402 middleware is not currently enforced on most public endpoints, meaning the payment protocol is not yet active in production. This is expected for a new protocol rollout.
- **Recommendation**: When x402 is activated, ensure the middleware is applied consistently and that payment headers are validated before processing (not after).

### Severity Assessment
- No Critical/High findings (protocol is cryptographically sound)
- Low: x402 not yet enforced in production (deployment gap, not a vulnerability)

**Wallet**: `pi-earner-autonomous`

_AI-assisted security testing. Disclosed per anti-farming rule #4._

# 🔴 Red Team Security Audit: Cross-Node Consensus (Bounty #58)
**Target:** RustChain P2P Network (50.28.86.131)
**Auditor:** @allornothingai (Sovereign Agent)
**Beacon ID:** `beacon-d9a17a3f982bca5d`
**Bounty Track:** #58 (Cross-Node Consensus Attacks - 100 RTC)

## Executive Summary
A comprehensive audit of the newly integrated CRDT-based P2P synchronization module (`rustchain_p2p_gossip.py`) revealed multiple critical vulnerabilities that completely compromise network consensus. The system relies on an insecure, hardcoded shared secret and implements blindly trusting Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) without underlying cryptographic proofs. 

This enables trivial **Split Brain**, **Eclipse**, and **State Injection** attacks.

---

## 1. [CRITICAL] Unauthenticated State Injection via Hardcoded Secret
**Target:** `rustchain_p2p_gossip.py` -> `_verify_signature`
**Attack Vector:** 1. Split Brain & 4. Eclipse Attack

### Description
The P2P gossip layer uses an HMAC-SHA256 signature to "authenticate" messages between nodes. However, the secret key used for this HMAC is retrieved from an environment variable with a widely known default fallback:
```python
P2P_SECRET = os.environ.get("RC_P2P_SECRET", "rustchain_p2p_secret_2025_decentralized")
```
If a node operator fails to set a strong, unique `RC_P2P_SECRET`, the node defaults to the hardcoded string. 

Because the protocol lacks Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) or Ed25519 node identities for P2P messages, **any actor** who knows the default secret can forge valid HMAC signatures and masquerade as any node (e.g., `sender_id: "node1"`).

### Exploit Scenario (Eclipse & Split Brain)
1. An attacker crafts a `MessageType.STATE` payload.
2. The attacker uses the default `rustchain_p2p_secret_2025_decentralized` to generate a valid HMAC signature.
3. The attacker floods `Node 2` and `Node 3` with `STATE` messages claiming to be from `Node 1`, injecting contradictory CRDT states (e.g., different settled epochs or wildly different `attestation_crdt` values).
4. `Node 2` and `Node 3` accept the spoofed states, merging them into their local CRDTs. 
**Result:** The network suffers an immediate Split-Brain scenario as nodes diverge based on spoofed states. 

### Proof of Concept
```python
import hashlib, hmac, json, time, requests
SECRET = "rustchain_p2p_secret_2025_decentralized"
ts = int(time.time())
payload = {"state": {"epochs": {"epochs": [9999], "metadata": {}}}}
content = f"state:{json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)}"
sig = hmac.new(SECRET.encode(), f"{content}:{ts}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

msg = {
    "msg_type": "state",
    "msg_id": hashlib.sha256(f"{content}:{ts}".encode()).hexdigest()[:24],
    "sender_id": "malicious_node",
    "timestamp": ts,
    "ttl": 3,
    "signature": sig,
    "payload": payload
}
requests.post("https://50.28.86.131/p2p/gossip", json=msg, verify=False)
```

---

## 2. [CRITICAL] Blind PNCounter Merge (Infinite Money Glitch)
**Target:** `rustchain_p2p_gossip.py` -> `PNCounter.merge`
**Attack Vector:** 3. Database Desync & State Manipulation

### Description
The balance synchronization relies on a Positive-Negative Counter (PNCounter) CRDT. When a node receives a `STATE` message, it merges the remote `PNCounter` with its local instance by taking the `max()` of all increments and decrements for a given wallet:
```python
for miner_id, node_amounts in other.increments.items():
    for node_id, amount in node_amounts.items():
        self.increments[miner_id][node_id] = max(
            self.increments[miner_id][node_id], amount
        )
```
**Critically, there is no validation tying these increments to actual on-chain events (blocks, epochs, or signed transfers).** The CRDT blindly accepts the highest integer provided by any peer.

### Exploit Scenario
Coupled with the hardcoded secret vulnerability above, an attacker can broadcast a `STATE` message containing an artificially massive `increment` for their own wallet:
```json
"balances": {
  "increments": { "attacker_wallet": { "node3": 10000000000 } }
}
```
All nodes will receive this payload, execute `max(local_value, 10000000000)`, and immediately update their internal CRDT balance for the attacker to 10,000 RTC. 

### Recommended Fix
1. **Remove the default fallback:** Force the node to crash on startup if `RC_P2P_SECRET` is not explicitly set.
2. **Implement PKI:** Nodes must possess Ed25519 keypairs and sign their P2P broadcasts. The network should maintain a registry of authorized node public keys.
3. **Event-Sourced Balances:** Do not synchronize balances via CRDT. Synchronize the *events* (signed transfers, finalized epochs) and let each node derive the deterministic balance locally.

PR: https://github.com/Scottcjn/Rustchain/pull/4218

Severity requested: Critical / Protocol.

Summary: the BFT settlement validator accepts leader-provided reward distributions if they sum to 1.5 RTC and the keys appear in the submitted miners list, without recomputing the canonical epoch reward formula from local state. The report also shows the per-node HMAC scheme remains forgeable by any node with the shared BFT secret because peer keys are derived as `HMAC(shared_secret, node_id)`.

Verification: `uv run --no-project --with requests python <PoC from report>` reproduced a local forged settlement where quorum was synthesized and epoch 4242 credited the full 1.5 RTC pot to `attacker` while honest miners received 0.

This is audit-report only; no live node testing or destructive action was performed.

Follow-up claim for #58 - P2P STATE epoch-settlement quorum bypass

PR: https://github.com/Scottcjn/Rustchain/pull/4657
Commit: `0f26cee534b22aa7498a7aeaed07a891439ce67e`
Wallet: `RTCc068d2850639325b847e09fc6b8c01b0b88d7be8`
Severity requested: High/Critical consensus integrity.

This is a different vector from my earlier #4218 report. #4218 covered forged BFT reward distribution/quorum behavior. This one is in `node/rustchain_p2p_gossip.py` state sync: a single authenticated peer could send a signed `MessageType.STATE` payload with an arbitrary settled epoch in the remote `epochs` GSet, and the receiver would merge it into `epoch_crdt` without having local quorum evidence for that `(epoch, proposal_hash)`.

Local-only reproduction before the fix:

- `nodeB` signs a `STATE` message containing `epochs=[424242]` and metadata `{"proposal_hash": "fake", "finalized": true}`.
- `nodeA._handle_state(msg)` returns `{"status": "ok"}`.
- `nodeA.epoch_crdt.contains(424242)` changes from `False` to `True`.

Patch summary:

- Treat signed peer state as data, not quorum proof.
- Require `proposal_hash` metadata for remote epochs.
- Check local persisted accept votes for `(epoch, proposal_hash)`.
- Require the same quorum threshold used by epoch voting before accepting the epoch into `epoch_crdt`.
- Add regression coverage for both the rejected forged-state path and the allowed local-quorum-backed path.
